clue.text: What detects flights heading east and west

definitions.text: What detects flights heading east and west

parts.note: the plain reading: the device that tracks aircraft
the hidden reading: a word that runs the same whichever way you head along it, a palindrome

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what device spots aircraft travelling in either direction.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across entry east is left-to-right and west right-to-left; the answer is a palindrome, so it reads identically both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Radar is the radio-wave system used by air traffic control to locate aircraft in the sky.

clue.text: Run over politician for a lark

parts.note: O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Someone runs over a politician just for fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is a carefree bit of fun or mischief, which is what a romp also means.

clue.text: Time spent in state of shock they say

indicators.note: signals that what we hear, not what is written, is wanted: a sound-alike

parts.note: a daze is a stunned, bewildered condition

explanation.surface: Someone reports a period spent in a stunned, shocked condition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Days' is a common expression for a span of time, as in 'my student days'.

clue.text: Resolve to out US president

indicators.note: the letters are put out of their order, like a dislocated joint

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A determination to remove an American head of state from office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolve to out' reads as a plan to oust a president, but 'out' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore and Franklin D. Roosevelt both held the office of President of the United States.

clue.text: Criminal admires his Smith & Wesson?

indicators.note: describes the letters as lawless, so they are rearranged rather than kept in order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gangster is fond of his revolver.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith & Wesson is a famous American gun maker, so the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidearm is a pistol or revolver carried at the belt, such as a Smith & Wesson handgun.

clue.text: Some Aussies taking an afternoon nap

indicators.note: only some of the letters in these words are used, a run concealed inside them

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A few Australians are having a snooze after lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is the customary midday or early-afternoon rest in hot countries.

clue.text: Director General eating duck — or some other creature?

indicators.note: one piece swallows the other, so the second goes inside the first

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, so it gives O

explanation.surface: A BBC chief tucks into duck, or perhaps some different animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Director General is the title of the head of the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog is an animal, the creature other than the duck the surface mentions.

clue.text: Bill has trade union friend, as it happens

parts.note: a bill is an account, abbreviated AC
an ally is a supporter or friend

explanation.surface: A man called Bill turns out to have a pal in the unions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is a bill to pay, an account.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Actually' is an adverb meaning in fact, the same sense as 'as it happens'.

clue.text: Display list of cargo on board

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to show or reveal
second meaning: the document listing a ship's freight

explanation.surface: A notice-board showing what a ship is carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for showing plainly and a noun for the shipping document detailing cargo.

clue.text: Can chap from Gdansk dance around this?

parts.note: 'may' expresses permission, like 'can'
Gdansk is in Poland, so the man is a Pole

explanation.surface: Asks whether a Polish man is able to dance round something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads naturally as a whole, but splits into permission plus a nationality, with the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A maypole is the tall ribboned pole that folk dancers circle on May Day.

clue.text: You need good school to succeed

parts.note: Eton is the famous English boarding school

explanation.surface: Advice that a decent education is required to do well in life.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is the elite English public school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on is a phrasal verb meaning to make progress or prosper in a career.

clue.text: Partner recovered, but not completely?

parts.note: someone who has recovered is better again
half of something is not the whole of it

explanation.surface: A spouse is getting well again, though only partly.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Better half' is a jocular idiom for one's wife, husband or spouse.

clue.text: Scoundrel meeting barrier in Dutch port

indicators.note: the two pieces come together side by side, one joining the next

parts.note: rotter is an old-fashioned word for a cad
a dam is a barrier holding back water

explanation.surface: A villain runs into a sea defence in a Netherlands harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam is the great seaport city of the Netherlands, among Europe's busiest harbours.

clue.text: Revolutionary a little crestfallen in Istanbul

indicators.note: only a small portion of these words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rebel feels somewhat downcast while in Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective but is a noun for a follower of Lenin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Leninist follows the communist doctrine of Lenin, leader of the Russian Revolution.

clue.text: Hunk of meat, followed by gateau

indicators.note: the first piece comes first and the next one after it

parts.note: beef is a meat
a gateau is a rich cake

explanation.surface: A lump of meat, with a fancy dessert for afters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunk of meat' reads as a chunk of food, but 'Hunk' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefcake is slang for a muscular, attractive man, which is what a hunk is.

clue.text: A number of the French caught in flat

indicators.note: one piece is trapped inside the other

parts.note: flat ground is level, or even
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A quantity of French people are found in an apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' tempts as an apartment, but here it means smooth and level.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a whole number, the integer one more than ten.

clue.text: Ancient writer's second lusty novel

definitions.note: read as 'ancient writer is', the 's being the verb

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer of old has a second, rather steamy book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylus was the pointed tool for inscribing wax tablets, the scribe's pen of the classical world.

clue.text: Outdo a single US gangster

parts.note: to cap something is to top or better it
one, a single item

explanation.surface: An American mobster tries to go one better than someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Capone was the notorious Chicago mob boss during Prohibition.

clue.text: Daft auntie hopelessly in love

indicators.note: the letters are in a hopeless muddle and must be sorted

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A silly aunt is besotted beyond help.
explanation.definitionFit: Infatuated means carried away by passion for someone, smitten.

clue.text: Local getting hold of E in Paddington?

indicators.note: the outer piece grips the other, which sits inside it

parts.note: in Britain one's local is one's nearby pub, or bar
taken as written

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood pub picks up an E in the London district of Paddington.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington is a London district and a station, but here is the marmalade-loving bear of children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddington is the fictional bear from Peru created by Michael Bond, so an example of the animal.

clue.text: Join an idiot, did you say?

indicators.note: asks what was heard, so a word with the same sound is wanted

parts.note: a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they were told to team up with a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to unite or fasten together, as bones knit after a break.

clue.text: I worried about Republican being very angry

indicators.note: the next piece comes around after, the Republican placed ahead of it

parts.note: taken as written
something that worried you ate at you

explanation.surface: Someone frets over a Republican and becomes furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ate' means troubled, as in 'what's eating you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate is an adjective meaning furious, full of rage.

clue.text: I pass at end of course

indicators.note: the final letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: the last letter of this word is the one taken
to go is to pass, as in 'time goes'

explanation.surface: A student says they will qualify when the course finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the subject of the sentence but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ego is the self, what a person means when saying 'I'.

clue.text: Not the freshest of vegetables, my friend

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a stale bean, literally
second meaning: a dated British form of address to a chum

explanation.surface: Addressing a mate while complaining about stale greens.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Old bean' is old-fashioned British slang for a pal, and literally a bean past its best.

clue.text: Hanging in there is old Penny

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: taken as the word there, used whole
P is the abbreviation for a penny in British money

explanation.surface: An elderly woman called Penny is hanging on bravely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hanging in there' suggests perseverance, but 'Hanging' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Execution by the noose is referred to as 'the rope', a euphemism for capital punishment by hanging.

clue.text: Queen visiting Massachusetts Institute of Technology? Goodness!

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside, so this piece sits within the other

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: The monarch tours an American university, prompting an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goodness!' looks like an exclamation but is the noun for virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Merit means worth or excellence, the quality of deserving praise.
